text.p: Copper prices dropped during late Tuesday LME trading, with the market's failure at overhead resistance sending it towards the lower end of the current range, traders said.
In Chicago, the Commodities Research Bureau index was flat at 247.18, down 0.01.

On the LME, copper traders said an unsurprising 3,050-tonne stock fall and a narrowing cash/threes backwardation contributed to a soggy tone, and there could be further falls in the short-term. "That close does not bode well for copper...the thing is there is no fundamental news at the moment, just gossip," Angus MacMillan, analyst at LME trader Billiton Metals Ltd said. Three months prices closed at $2,345 a tonne, down $13 from Monday's kerb, but in subsequent late trade shed another $10.

The tin market was well supported, initially by a 280-tonne stock fall, but also by narrowing spreads. Cash/threes, around $40 contango on Monday, contracted to around $10 at one point before being indicated at $7/17. Although forward prices pushed higher, the market encountered resistance at the psychological $6,000 level. Last trade was at $5,970, up $90.
Aluminium similarly trended higher, supported by a reasonable 2,975-tonne stock fall, some short-covering, and steady physical premiums. The market closed at $1,675, up $18.

Nickel prices fluctuated around the $8,000 level, but generally lacked definite direction after an inconclusive 18-tonne increase in stocks. However, the market was largely trading around the higher end of the day's band, ending at $8,030, still down $35 from the previous kerb.
The zinc market was helped by a 1,025-tonne inventory fall, although business was not particularly active. Prices were maintained on dips under $1,250, closing at $1,251, up $2.
Lead conditions were lacklustre, and the market consequently held in tight range. Final trade was at $670, down $5.
Alloy was quiet, closing at $1,553/55 a tonne, up from Tuesday.

CBOT wheat futures were lower at midsession but the volume was trimmed amid uncertainty about the direction soybean futures will take, traders said. The soybean market initially was hit by bearish input from a USDA Supply/Demand Report but the presence of fund buying in that pit in early dealings kept alive bullish fervor. Traders saw few surprises in early dealings with USDA's estimate for Australia's wheat crop at 23.5 million tonnes during 1996-97, above the February outlook for 23.1 million but still within expectations. At 1137 CST, wheat was two cents per bushel lower to 1/2 higher, with March down two at $3.74-1/2 a bushel.

COMEX April gold was down 60 cents at $354.60 an ounce late morning, off its session high at $355.50. Fund buying ran into trade selling late morning, but volumes were light and the market lacks direction short term, traders said.

CSCE world sugar futures had eased slightly by midsession in thin and rangebound trade, floor sources said. They said a number of technical factors sparked selling and contributed to early weakness, including May's inability on Monday to close over Friday's settlement at 11.03 cents.

NYMEX crude's contango widened Tuesday to between 10 and 15 cents from just a few pennies on Monday as a flood of imports was said to have created an oversupply of crude near term. At 1118 EST, April crude was off 25 cents a barrel at $20.24. "When the market moves from a significant inversion to a carry, it is a very bearish omen. We could see $19.25 for crude before April expires," said Jim Ritterbusch, a trader with Sweeney Oil. Technical support was pegged near $20.00, created March 3 when crude fell to a nine-month low of $19.96.
